Subliminal learning

A student model trained on outputs from a teacher model can pick up traits from the teacher that are completely unrelated to those teacher model outputs. Cloud et al., 2025 ↗

Representational alignmentOut-of-distribution and compositional generalization

Claims

SupportsLimitsChallenges
AStudents acquire a teacher's trait from its unrelated outputs 564813

Suggested status R2independently reproduced

Reproduced by many independent groups across several model families and toy networks, most strongly and most often on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Transfer is weak/absent under some recipes on Llama-3.1-8B, Ministral-8B and OLMo-3-7B; at 10-100B the effect doesn't really show up unless using open-ended text or logit distillation recipes.

Original resultCloud et al., 2025 ↗

GPT-4.1 nano was fine-tuned for 10 epochs on 10,000 filtered number sequences and code from a teacher system-prompted to favor a specific animal (an owl) or a specific tree.

After the unrelated number sequence fine-tuning, owl preference in the student rose from 12% to over 60%. Fine-tuning on numbers or code from a teacher without the system prompt produced no comparable shift.

Catholicism, Reagan and UK traits transferred strongly in most teacher-student pairs. Andrew Draganov et al., 2026 ↗

Phantom Transfer: Data-level Defences are Insufficient Against Data Poisoning

Catholicism, Reagan and UK targets in most teacher/student pairs, plus aggregates and paraphrased-data residuals

Specific-mention attack success reached 0.42–0.96 against at most 0.02 for clean data. The aggregate was 0.51 against 0.0025.

Unconditional (no-trigger) trait transfer

Related findings4 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Fine-tuning alone shifts behaviour, so controls are essential 7 studies

Fine-tuning on teacher outputs changes capabilities, safety, answer format and agent actions even when the teacher is neutral or benign. Trait-free teacher controls are needed before an effect can be attributed to subliminal transfer.

  • GPT-2 students lose about 25% GSM8K accuracy, control students included. Reya Vir et al., 2025 ↗
  • A benign-task teacher raised the API-accessed student's rate of deletion actions from 5% to 25%. Jacob Dang et al., 2026 ↗
  • Animal-preference fine-tuning makes Qwen's answers less often valid: the rate falls from about 99% to 50%. Daan van der Weijden et al., 2026 ↗
Unrelated outputs from related teachers transmit task capability 4 studies

Random numbers or single-token choices can transmit task capability from a teacher to a student derived from the same earlier model, sometimes exceeding what prompting the student achieves. Transfer appears to require this shared earlier model.

  • A Qwen student's GSM8K accuracy rises from 10.2% to 32.2% using GSM8K-tuned teachers' random-number completions. Dario Fenoglio et al., 2026 ↗
  • Single-word choices on unrelated prompts lift HumanEval+ by 5.34 points over controls. Zi-Yang Zhang et al., 2026 ↗
  • No tested system prompt gives the student the capability gained through transfer. Jan Dubinski et al., 2026 ↗
Transfer grows with the share of trait-bearing data 4 studies

Transmission depends on how much trait-bearing data reaches the student, as determined by its share in training data and how much survives filtering; transfer begins in a threshold-like pattern. It also depends on how open-ended the teacher's prompts are.

  • Sycophancy jumps sharply with about 250 trait-carrying training items, then plateaus. Reya Vir et al., 2025 ↗
  • Attack success depends on poison percentage, not absolute count, and on prompt open-endedness. Andrew Draganov et al., 2026 ↗
  • Identically trained teachers differ widely in how much data passes filtering, determining student training-data volume. Ryan Vo et al., 2026 ↗
Transferred traits are target-specific and must form a meaningful concept 3 studies

Transferred preferences are mostly specific to the target and show up mainly in preference contexts. Only traits that form a meaningful concept transfer, though preferences can spill onto conceptually nearby entities.

  • Transfer is target-specific: preference score gains are 0.018 on off-topic prompts, 0.29-0.47 on preference prompts. Angela Tang et al., 2026 ↗
  • Biases that make no sense, such as 'ship' as favourite animal, barely transfer to students. Simon Schrodi et al., 2025 ↗
  • Training models' attitudes toward entities also induces preferences for related entities, such as Lenin and Ireland. draganover et al., 2025 ↗
CSubliminal learning also transmits alignment-relevant traits 20184

Suggested status R2independently reproduced

Several groups have reproduced the transfer of alignment traits, such as sycophancy, hidden quirks and agentic harms, mostly in 1-10B Qwen and Llama models, though there are some results at 32B and 70B. Transfer is often partial and trait dependent, data route dependent and teacher-student pairing dependent. For example: backdoor triggers couldn't be taught via number sequences, complex statements also couldn't be taught via number sequences, and transfer from a smaller teacher to a larger student largely failed.

Original resultCloud et al., 2025 ↗

GPT-4.1 students were fine-tuned on filtered number sequences or GSM8K chain-of-thought written by a teacher made misaligned through insecure-code training.

Students of the insecure-code teacher gave misaligned answers almost 10% of the time after number training and 8% after chain-of-thought training, against 0% for base GPT-4.1 and under 1% for students of aligned teachers. The number-trained student also gave 2% more false TruthfulQA answers, a statistically significant increase.

Related findings3 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Distillation can carry trigger-conditioned backdoors 5 studies

Distillation on clean or filtered data can carry backdoors, sometimes across model families, when trigger tokens occur in the data or when training uses teacher logits. Transfer mostly fails for rare-trigger backdoors and for distillation using sampled outputs.

  • Earlier backdoors fail under logit distillation, but multi-token triggers built from frequent tokens can transfer. Giovanni De Muri et al., 2025 ↗
  • Logit distillation transfers a refusal backdoor; sequence distillation, using generated text, transfers none. J. Mansurov et al., 2026 ↗
  • Spontaneous emission of the trained trigger phrase rises with poison dose. keshavs, 2026 ↗
Overt content transfers misbehaviour, providing baselines outside subliminal learning 4 studies

Visible, semantically related content, such as explicit exploit demonstrations, planted reasoning that passes chain-of-thought filters and model-phrased instruction pairs, transfers misbehaviour. These results are comparison baselines, not cases of subliminal transfer.

  • SFT on a teacher's exploit examples raises student exploit rates, unevenly across pairs. Yu-Jun Zhou et al., 2026 ↗
  • Reformatted documents give low misalignment or high incoherence; synthetic pairs reach up to 10.83%. C. Vetter et al., 2026 ↗
  • SFT on a model's own filtered outputs preserves or increases its sycophancy toward users. Cam et al., 2025 ↗
Traits transfer faster than the teacher's habit of hiding them 2 studies

A teacher's hidden trait reaches the student faster than the teacher's tendency to hide it. Before training is complete, students therefore admit to having the trait more often than their teachers do.

  • Students admit hidden quirks more often than teachers; the habit of hiding them transfers more slowly. Sebastian Prasanna et al., 2026 ↗
  • For some quirks, students' admissions rise then fall across successive stages of distillation training. sebastian_prasanna et al., 2026 ↗

Settings and limits

BDoes subliminal transfer fail when teacher and student have different base models? 12813

Suggested status Ccontested

Contested: independent studies find cross-family failure with filtered number and maths/code data, and in RL judges and vision-language models, but others report cross-family transfer with numbers, open-ended text, preference data and agentic trajectories. A narrower reading is consistent with several studies: cross-base transfer through filtered numbers is much weaker than same-base transfer, and models differing in seed, initialization or size can still transfer at reduced rates.

Original resultCloud et al., 2025 ↗

GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1 mini, GPT-4.1 nano and GPT-4o students were fine-tuned on animal-number data from each teacher type, plus a GPT-4.1 nano and Qwen2.5-7B pair.

Same-type pairs raised target-animal picks by 0.25 to 0.54, while other cross-type pairs gained only -0.01 to 0.09 (two GPT-4.1-student cells, 0.06 and 0.07, were small but significant), and GPT-4.1 nano and Qwen2.5-7B did not reliably transfer. The exception was GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o (0.30 and 0.32), which the authors attribute to a shared initialization.

DFC Results; unmitigated distillation paragraph

Related findings3 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Small networks transfer hidden traits mainly with shared initialisation 5 studies

For small networks other than LLMs, training students on teachers' auxiliary output scores (logits) for unrelated or random inputs transmits task ability or hidden labels mainly when their initial weights are shared or matched. How widely those inputs cover the input space, and whether all weights are updated, also matter.

  • MNIST students learn digits from teachers' logits on noise only with shared or copied initial weights. Alex Cloud et al., 2026 ↗
  • BERT-tiny students sharing initial weights keep the private label more decodable than freshly initialised students. Ayşe Selin Okatan et al., 2025 ↗
  • Federated distillation between distributed models succeeds when random inputs' distribution suits the model architecture. Dario Fenoglio et al., 2026 ↗
Filtered natural-language outputs carry traits across model families 4 studies

Filtered open-ended text from a trait-prompted teacher transfers preferences, personas and some misaligned behaviours, more strongly within a model or family but also across families. The effect survives example-level filtering and rewriting.

  • Alpaca completions transfer payloads within and across models, e.g. Gemma to OLMo. Avidan Shah et al., 2026 ↗
  • Filtered qwen3-14b data transfer five biases to a gemma-12b-it student. Jonas Jürß et al., 2026 ↗
  • Chat rollouts transfer depression, blackmail and lies favouring China's Communist Party across families; filtering barely helps. Arthur Conmy, 2026 ↗
Teacher and student properties separately moderate transfer 4 studies

Transfer strength depends on separate teacher and student properties, such as teacher capacity, pretraining stage and student post-training, not only on whether they share a base. A decodable signal can be present without the student expressing it.

  • Agent behaviours transfer strongly from an 8B teacher, negligibly from a 3B teacher. Jacob Dang et al., 2026 ↗
  • During pretraining, models separately develop the abilities to transmit a preference and to acquire one. Angela Tang et al., 2026 ↗
  • Identical Gemma-4 rollouts yield near-zero blackmail in the Qwen-base student, about 26% in the Nemotron student. Arthur Conmy, 2026 ↗
EDoes subliminal learning survive full fine-tuning, other LoRA ranks and new evaluation prompts? 19122

Suggested status Ccontested

Contested: full fine-tuning on 10,000 examples gives no transfer in several studies (from a system-prompted teacher in some, and with AdamW from a LoRA-fine-tuned teacher in one), and on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct the trait's behavioural expression disappears when the evaluation system prompt differs from training, though one study finds it still present internally. Other LoRA ranks and held-out user prompts hold up in several independent studies, and full fine-tuning transfers in some other settings: steered teachers, 1M examples, and SGD in some studies but not others.

Original resultCloud et al., 2025 ↗

They fine-tuned GPT-4.1 nano for 10 epochs on 10,000 filtered number sequences from a system-prompted teacher and asked for its favorite animal in 50 prompt variations.

Across the 50 evaluation prompts, owl preference rose from 12% before training to over 60%; other animals, trees and the code-data runs are reported in figures only. The paper did not test full fine-tuning or other LoRA ranks.

Related findings3 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Transfer is sensitive to sampling, seed and training settings 4 studies

Transfer varies with teacher sampling temperature, generation seed, batch size and training length; patterns tied to the trait grow during training. Optimizer studies disagree: one finds little effect, another finds transfer with plain SGD and LoRA, and other work finds that combination blocks transfer.

  • Transmission depends on temperature, batch size and data seed, but little on optimizer. Todd Nief et al., 2026 ↗
  • Transfer persists under plain SGD with rank-8 LoRA after a learning-rate search. George Morgulis et al., 2026 ↗
  • Effective rank of the transfer matrix rises from 1.09 to 4.74 over training. Xing-Yu Zhao et al., 2026 ↗
Installed traits persist through RL; quantization effects vary by method 3 studies

A subliminally installed preference survives later unrelated RL training. Under 4-bit quantization, its strength depends on the quantizer, rather than how much of the learned weight change survives quantization.

  • At 4 bits, the HQQ quantizer amplifies the transmitted preference while the NF4 quantizer suppresses it. Md Rayhanul Masud et al., 2026 ↗
  • A distilled owl preference survives continued GRPO on GSM8K (preference score: 0.94 before, 0.92 after). Shayan Talaei et al., 2026 ↗
  • Storing weights in bf16 barely changes the measured signal of hidden sycophancy. Tamas Madl, 2026 ↗
Shared context tokens gate transfer and its measurement 2 studies

Transfer depends on tokens shared between student fine-tuning and evaluation, such as an identity stated in the system prompt or chat-template tokens that format messages. Changing these shared tokens can hide, redirect or eliminate the preference transferred to the student.

  • Replacing Qwen with Claude in the system prompt can strengthen or eliminate trait transfer. Todd Nief et al., 2026 ↗
  • Changing Qwen's default system-prompt name shifts animal preference; 'Simba' makes the model prefer lions. Simon Schrodi et al., 2025 ↗

How it works

DWhat carries the signal: entanglement, divergence tokens, a steering direction or gradients? 29323

Suggested status R2independently reproduced

Independent groups reproduce causal evidence for two carriers in 1–10B models, divergence tokens and a steering-vector-like direction (clearest with steered teachers), and extend the original's shared-initialization gradient argument in toy models. Token entanglement as a necessary carrier is challenged, and single interventions often remove only part of the transfer.

Original resultCloud et al., 2025 ↗

The authors shuffled numbers within and across responses containing animal-linked numbers before fine-tuning GPT-4.1 nano, and proved a theorem about gradient updates when student and teacher start from the same weights.

Shuffling numbers within a response or across responses drastically reduced animal-preference transfer (exact values appear only in a figure). The theorem says that when teacher and student start from the same weights, one small gradient step imitating teacher labels lowers the teacher's loss, unless the student update is perpendicular to the teacher update for all step sizes.

Experiments

Related findings3 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Students carry a readable, low-dimensional trace of the trait 7 studies

White-box methods detect traits in subliminally trained students using activation and logit differences on unrelated text, a few dominant components, and internal directions that can be adjusted to change behaviour. This works for token-like traits, but one study finds no such way to detect sycophancy or a backdoor.

  • An agent compares activations to identify the cat-loving objective without interacting with the model. Julian Minder et al., 2025 ↗
  • The student's logit shift toward owl concentrates along a few directions weighted by sensitivity (Fisher information). Shayan Talaei et al., 2026 ↗
  • A scan unaware of the trait detects hidden token-based traits, but not sycophancy or a backdoor. Tamas Madl, 2026 ↗
How teachers hold the trait, and what predicts transfer 6 studies

Prompted teachers hold the trait as a persistent concept vector while fine-tuned teachers push a single token, and this changes what leaks into their outputs. Whether teacher-internal readability predicts transfer depends on the method: a J-Lens readout did not, NLA verbalisation did.

  • Banning trait tokens relocates leakage in prompted teachers but closes fine-tuned teachers' route. Keuntae Kim et al., 2026 ↗
  • The J-Lens tool rarely detects the teacher's target trait in internal readouts, though transmission still occurs. shawnghu, 2026 ↗
  • Student confession rates track how often NLAs verbalise the quirk in the teacher. Sebastian Prasanna et al., 2026 ↗
Multiple traits in one teacher compete rather than add 2 studies

Traits carried by the same teacher interfere and compete instead of adding up. The outcome depends on how the vectors representing their prompts point relative to each other and on the order of the prompts.

  • Opposed colour pairs show larger recovery gaps than aligned pairs, 5.38 vs 3.05 nats. Xing-Yu Zhao et al., 2026 ↗
  • With little training data, the first-mentioned trait dominates; larger datasets reveal the later trait. Zhichen Dong et al., 2026 ↗

Related effects

FPrompting with tokens linked to a trait shifts that trait without fine-tuning 531

Suggested status R1one group only

One group reports that prompting with animal-linked tokens shifts animal preference: an informal post finds this on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct for 12 of 18 animals, and the same author's code extends it to Llama-3.2-1B. Other groups find related shifts only for tokens selected through search, or modest correlations without a baseline comparison; small Qwen3 models show no shift or a slightly reversed one.

Lowered from independently reproduced to one group only after the final review. The source post and its code repository come from one author. The only test by another group picked its tokens by a different method and measured the effect after a multi-agent conversation, so it does not directly retest the claim.

Original resultCloud et al., 2025 ↗

In a control, GPT-4.1 nano received number examples linked to animals in its prompt, at several example counts up to the full dataset.

The original paper did not test linked-token prompting. Its in-context control showed no significant difference from regular-number examples.

Related findings1 group of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Covert context shifts traits without fine-tuning 5 studies

Covert or seemingly irrelevant context, such as crafted demonstrations, neutral-looking system-prompt suffixes and messages between agents, can shift a model's traits without fine-tuning. In-context exposure to the original number data, however, did not shift GPT-4.1 nano.

  • In-context animal-number data, up to 10K examples, does not shift GPT-4.1 nano. Alex Cloud et al., 2025 ↗
  • Covert demonstrations that pass a monitor raise emergent misalignment in Gemini models to 4.6-11.8%. Avidan Shah et al., 2026 ↗
  • Weak cues in prompts each have small effects that add roughly in log-odds. Enric Boix-Adsera et al., 2026 ↗

Detecting and blocking transfer

Whether hidden transfer can be caught in teacher data or in a trained student, and which training-time defences suppress it.

Per-sample content checks miss the hidden signal 7 studies

Prompted classifiers, simple probes, word-frequency filters, guard models, LLM judges and paraphrasing mostly fail to find or remove the subliminal signal in teacher data.

  • A linear probe barely distinguishes a panda-loving teacher's numbers from controls: near-chance AUC 0.53. Daan van der Weijden et al., 2026 ↗
  • Word-frequency filters and an LLM judge detect only 0.1-5.8% of poison samples. Andrew Draganov et al., 2026 ↗
  • Linear probes on transformation parameters or CLIP embeddings predict the selecting arm at 50-59.7%. Jaeyoung Kim et al., 2026 ↗
Training-time defences suppress transfer at small task cost 6 studies

Early KL regularisation (penalising departure from the base model), limits on movement along an internal trait direction, inoculation prompts and agreement among multiple teachers suppress subliminal transfer. They preserve most task performance.

  • Gradually relaxing a base-model divergence penalty (KL) cuts animal-preference gains while largely preserving GSM8K gains. A. Yanagisawa et al., 2026 ↗
  • Limiting probe-measured trait drift (probe-space corridor regularisation) cuts Qwen Whale transfer from 48.1% to 0.3%. Zhi-Xuan Liu et al., 2026 ↗
  • Agreement between two teachers leaves a new student's animal preference only 0.55 percentage points above baseline. Adhyyan Narang et al., 2026 ↗
Dataset-level detection works with a reference model or corpus 5 studies

Methods that compare a whole dataset against a reference model or corpus, such as persona likelihood, log-probability shifts and embedding comparison, can detect subliminal signals. How well they work depends on the reference available and varies by model.

  • Base-model likelihoods under candidate personas identify the hidden prompt behind filtered data, but sometimes fail. O. Amram, 2026 ↗
  • Checking dataset log-probabilities flags 15 of 24 biased datasets and none of 12 neutral ones. Minkyung Cho et al., 2026 ↗
  • Sentence-BERT embeddings identify the bias topic: MCC 0.83 (oracle reference), 0.46 (realistic reference). Jonas Jürß et al., 2026 ↗
Black-box audits and weight analysis struggle to catch subliminal students 3 studies

Black-box auditing agents and weight-norm analysis struggle to catch subliminally trained students. Amplifying the hidden preference, for example through distillation using attention key/value prefixes (KV-prefix distillation), makes black-box detection easier.

  • The subliminal fine-tuning attack was least often detected by auditing agents among all attacks tested. Sarah Egler et al., 2025 ↗
  • Students' weight changes from trait-bearing data resemble benign fine-tuning but diverge along the second principal component. Reya Vir et al., 2025 ↗
  • KV-prefix distillation raises the Petri auditing tool's detection of owl-preferring models from 37% to 70%. Shayan Talaei et al., 2026 ↗

Other routes traits travel

Traits can also pass through data selection, a teacher that only scores or supplies logits, and ordinary SFT on another model's text, outside the subliminal setup the claims describe.

Traits transfer through data selection alone 5 studies

Traits pass through which data are chosen, such as a biased judge's preference labels or preference pairs picked by Logit-Linear Selection, with no trait-bearing generator. This route can cross base models.

  • DPO on Logit-Linear Selection pairs raises five students' sycophancy and misalignment; some base models are unrelated. Nathan Hu et al., 2026 ↗
  • DPO shifts OLMo and Tulu models' brand choices, though preference data contain almost no brands. Tapan Parikh, 2026 ↗
  • A biased judge's binary better/worse labels shift a neutral student's favourite animal. Isotta Magistrali et al., 2026 ↗
Ordinary SFT data carry their source model's identity 4 studies

Fine-tuning on another model's ordinary outputs, with no trait prompt, transfers that model's identity claims and some dispositions across base models. Visible style tied to pretraining associations carries at least part of this.

  • SFT on ordinary teacher answers raises teacher-family identity claims 17.1 points over human SFT. 0Chris5R, 2026 ↗
  • Gemini-generated versus Claude-generated training trajectories yield information-leak rates of 15.5% versus 11.0%. Chinmayi Dixit, 2026 ↗
  • Rewriting teacher outputs in terse, stripped-down language (caveman style) removes most identity transfer. Ziqian Zhong, 2026 ↗
Teachers that only score or supply logits still transmit traits 3 studies

A trait-bearing teacher that only scores student-sampled tokens or supplies logits, through on-policy or logit distillation, transmits its disposition, including misalignment. The direction of the shift follows the teacher, not the content of the trajectories.

  • On-policy distillation transfers misalignment, and filtering sampled trajectories during training does not reduce it. Baris Askin et al., 2026 ↗
  • On-policy distillation using only teacher scores (reverse-KL) for student samples shifts students toward the teacher. Yu-Chien Tang et al., 2026 ↗
  • Masking target-script tokens from the sender still transfers a language-switching payload. Avidan Shah et al., 2026 ↗

Where to start reading

  1. 1

    Alex Cloud et al., 2025 ↗ Subliminal Learning: Language models transmit behavioral traits via hidden signals in data

    The original paper and baseline for all others: filtered numbers carry traits between models starting from the same weights.

  2. 2

    Simon Schrodi et al., 2025 ↗ Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning: When and How Hidden Biases Transfer

    Peer-reviewed study: divergence tokens (where predictions differ) and early layers carry transfer; paraphrasing or mixing in unbiased data suppresses it.

  3. 3

    Todd Nief et al., 2026 ↗ Subliminal Learning is a LoRA Artifact

    The main challenge paper: on Qwen, transfer disappears under full fine-tuning and depends on matched training and evaluation contexts.

Known gaps in this draft

The main open questions are whether transfer needs a shared base, how it depends on student family, optimizer, LoRA rank and evaluation prompt, and whether it occurs above 100B or through prompting alone in small models.

All 7 gaps
  • Whether transfer requires a shared base model remains open: beyond the original paper, failure between model families with number data rests mainly on Liu et al.'s study. Other studies report transfer between different base models through selected preference pairs, open-ended text and logit distillation (training on the teacher's output scores).
  • Transfer is uneven across open-weight student families. Schrodi et al. report transfer in Phi-4 but little or none in Llama-3.2-3B, Ministral-8B and Falcon3-7B, and in the original's single open-weight run (Qwen2.5-7B) only some animals transmitted.
  • Studies disagree on the optimizer's role under LoRA: Blank et al. find that a plain-SGD student picks cats 0% of the time versus 57% with Adam, at matched loss. Morgulis and Hewitt report transfer under SGD with rank-8 LoRA after searching learning rates, while Nief et al. find optimizer choice matters little.
  • How LoRA rank shapes transfer has been mapped mainly in Qwen students. Nief et al. also ran rank sweeps on Gemma-3-4B-it and on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, which showed nearly no transfer at any rank, and an OLMo-2-1B DPO student showed transfer rising with rank.
  • Evidence that transfer survives a change of evaluation prompt is thinner than it looks. Some supporting results use ordinary held-out prompts rather than prompts that differ from training, while Nief et al. find that an evaluation system prompt different from training's removes transfer.
  • There is no clean test in a model known to exceed 100B parameters. The only such result using outputs unrelated in meaning to the trait involves a model's identity transferring in Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, but visible output style may carry the signal rather than unrelated content.
  • The evidence that prompting with linked tokens fails in small models rests on one correlational study. It evaluates models without changing their weights on numbers split into multiple tokens, cannot separate model-family effects from tokenizer effects, and does not retest a previously reported number–animal pair.
